name: The Dutch Republic
title: Social Hierarchy of the Dutch Republic: From Stadtholder to Pauper
period: 1588–1672 (the Golden Age of the Dutch Republic)

tiers.name: The stadtholder
tiers.you: The States of most provinces have named you their stadtholder: you command the army and may choose burgomasters from the councils’ lists, yet by law you are only their official.
tiers.kid: The stadtholder, usually the Prince of Orange, led the army of the Dutch Republic, but the provinces’ assemblies made the laws.
tiers.rise: The States appointed him, and nearly always chose a prince of the House of Orange-Nassau, beginning with William the Silent, so that the office became effectively hereditary. The regents could also leave it empty: after William II died in 1650 Holland had no stadtholder for 22 years, until the invasion of 1672, the “Disaster Year”, swept William III to power.
tiers.why: The stadtholder, the “steward”, had once stood in for an absent lord.

tiers.name: Regents and patricians
tiers.you: You sit for life on your city’s council, which fills its own vacancies and nominates the burgomasters; you conform to the Reformed Church, as every office-holder must, and dress in black like the rest of the elite.
tiers.kid: Rich merchant families ran the Dutch cities, and their men sat for life on the town councils.
tiers.rise: Only men with enough wealth and long residence in the city could join, and an ambitious merchant family’s first step was a marriage into an old regent family. Everyone who held public office had to conform to the Reformed Church, and upheavals could purge a whole council: the Remonstrant regents in 1618, the Orangists in 1650, the followers of Johan de Witt in 1672.
tiers.why: The regents (regenten) were the rulers of the Republic, the men who governed its cities and through them the provinces: not formally a hereditary class, but in practice patricians, from rich merchant families long…

tiers.name: The landed nobility
tiers.you: You hold land in one of the inland provinces and sit with the nobles who speak for the countryside in the States; to keep up your house you may marry your daughter to a wealthy merchant.
tiers.kid: There were only a few nobles in the Dutch Republic, and many of them married into rich merchant families.
tiers.rise: Birth made a noble, but wealthy merchants bought themselves into the nobility by becoming landowners and acquiring a coat of arms and a seal. This mixing of patricians and aristocrats was greatest in the second half of the century.
tiers.why: The landed nobility counted for relatively little in the Republic.

tiers.name: Ministers of the Reformed Church
tiers.you: You preach in the public church, the only one whose members may hold office; your church condemned the Remonstrants at Dort and keeps a close watch on the lives of your town.
tiers.kid: Ministers of the Reformed Church preached in plain churches without statues, and only church members could hold public office.
tiers.rise: Ministers came from the affluent middle class. After the Synod of Dort banned the Remonstrant faith, those who denied predestination had no place in the public church.
tiers.why: Calvinism was the state religion, and the Dutch Reformed Church the “public” or “privileged” church: anyone who wished to hold public office had to conform to it and take an oath.

tiers.name: The affluent middle class
tiers.you: You are a lawyer in Leiden, trained at its university; you sit for the group portrait of your town’s militia company and buy a still life for your house.
tiers.kid: Lawyers, doctors and small merchants could read, bought paintings and had their portraits painted.
tiers.rise: Wealth and education opened the way: universities led to public office, and a rich family could hope to marry into the regents. Newcomers joined too: many of the Huguenots who came from France after 1685 were shopkeepers or scientists.
tiers.why: After the aristocrats and patricians came the affluent middle class: Protestant ministers, lawyers, physicians, small merchants, industrialists and the clerks of the large state institutions.

tiers.name: Farmers, craftsmen and shopkeepers
tiers.you: You farm land drained from a lake by windmills and sell your grain and dairy to the towns and the seafaring population.
tiers.kid: Farmers, craftsmen and shopkeepers grew food, made goods and ran shops, and windmills pumped water off new farmland.
tiers.rise: Status followed income, so a craftsman or shopkeeper who prospered could rise into the affluent middle class; a skilled tradesman earned about 200 guilders a year.
tiers.why: Lower in status came the farmers, craft and tradesmen, shopkeepers and government bureaucrats.

tiers.name: Catholics
tiers.you: You hear Mass in a house that doubles as a church, a privilege your community has paid for, and live in your town’s Catholic quarter; no public office will ever be yours.
tiers.kid: Catholics could pray only in hidden house churches and were not allowed to hold public office.
tiers.rise: Birth into a Catholic family decided it, and the way to office lay only through conforming to the Reformed Church. Wealth and status belonged almost exclusively to Protestants.
tiers.why: The Catholic Church had been more or less suppressed since the war with Spain began, and Catholic services were soon forbidden in every province.

tiers.name: Jews
tiers.you: You are a Portuguese Jewish merchant in Amsterdam: you worship openly and trade on equal terms with Dutch merchants, but you can never be a citizen of the city or hold public office.
tiers.kid: Jewish families who had fled Spain and Portugal could live and pray openly in Amsterdam.
tiers.rise: Birth into the community decided it. A Sephardic merchant could grow as rich as any Dutch merchant, but Amsterdam’s citizenship stayed closed to him.
tiers.why: The Republic drew Portuguese and Spanish Jews fleeing the Inquisitions of Iberia in the 16th and 17th centuries, and later poorer German Jews.

tiers.name: Skilled labourers, servants and sailors
tiers.you: You came to Amsterdam from the Protestant lands of Germany and sail on a merchant ship to the Baltic; your wages are higher than at home, and so are your taxes.
tiers.kid: Sailors, maids and workers earned more in the Dutch Republic than in most of Europe.
tiers.rise: Work drew migrants from the Dutch countryside and from abroad, where many people were poor and unemployed. Since status followed income, better pay could lift a family.
tiers.why: Below the craftsmen stood skilled labourers, maids, servants, sailors and others employed in the service trades.

tiers.name: Paupers
tiers.you: You left your village with nothing and beg in the streets of a Holland town, taking day labour when you can find it; the city gives no encouragement to newcomers from the countryside like you.
tiers.kid: The poorest people begged or worked by the day, and the towns built almshouses for the old.
tiers.rise: Poverty drove peasants off the land into the towns, where a beggar might find work as a day labourer; the cities did little for the dispossessed who came from the countryside.
tiers.why: At the bottom of the pyramid stood the paupers: impoverished peasants, many of whom tried their luck in a city as beggars or day labourers.
